title: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
summary: How vLLM plugs FlashAttention, FlashInfer, Triton, FlashMLA and CPU kernels behind one interface: selection, mixed batches, the forward pass, FP8 and hybrid caches, CUDA graphs.
outcomes: Explain the roles of AttentionBackend, AttentionMetadataBuilder and AttentionImpl in one vLLM step, and write a minimal one
Predict which backend vLLM selects for a given GPU, model and flags, and why an explicit choice can fail
Trace how a mixed prefill/decode batch is reordered, split and handed to different kernels
Trace one layer's cache write and varlen kernel call, with the value of every metadata tensor
Compute KV page bytes, block table sizes, slot numbers and CUDA graph padding for a configuration
Explain how FP8 scales reach the cache write and the kernel, and which backends accept which FP8 formats
Explain how hybrid models give each KV cache group its own block table, builder and possibly backend
Explain how AttentionCGSupport limits CUDA graph modes and when vLLM downgrades them

lessons.title: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction

blocks.md:
vLLM runs on Ampere, Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, on AMD GPUs and on CPUs. It serves models with grouped-query attention (GQA), DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention (MLA), sliding windows and attention sinks, with KV caches in BF16 or FP8. Each of these changes what an attention kernel has to do:

- GQA lets a group of query heads share one key-value (KV) head. Llama-3-8B has 32 query heads but only 8 KV heads, so its cache is 4 times smaller than with one KV head per query head.
- MLA, introduced with DeepSeek-V2, caches one compressed latent vector per token instead of per-head keys and values: in DeepSeek-V3, 512 numbers plus a 64-number key part that carries the rotary position embedding. Each head rebuilds its keys and values from that latent.

- A sliding window lets each token attend only to the most recent W tokens instead of the whole context.
- An attention sink, as in gpt-oss, is a learned extra score per head that sits in the softmax denominator, so a head can put its weight on nothing. (Not StreamingLLM's sink tokens, the first few cached tokens that some compression methods keep: this sink is a learned number, not a token.)
- BF16 (brain floating point, named after Google Brain, which designed it) is a 16-bit float with float32's 8 exponent bits but only 7 fraction bits. FP8 stores each number in a single byte instead of two, which halves the cache again.

No single attention kernel covers that whole space. vLLM wraps each kernel library in a backend named after it: FlashAttention; FlashInfer, a kernel library built for LLM serving; Triton, OpenAI's Python-based language for writing GPU kernels; CUTLASS (CUDA Templates for Linear Algebra Subroutines), NVIDIA's C++ library of matrix-multiply building blocks; and FlashMLA, DeepSeek's open-source kernels for MLA decoding.

The source is explicit about the limits. The FlashMLA backend accepts only compute capability (NVIDIA's GPU architecture version: 8.x Ampere, 9.x Hopper, 10.x data-center Blackwell) 9.x or 10.x and a kernel block size (tokens per KV cache block) of exactly 64. `CUTLASS_MLA` accepts only 10.x and blocks of 128. `TRITON_ATTN` accepts any compute capability, which makes it the usual fallback. So vLLM separates *what* a layer computes (attention over a paged KV cache) from *how* (a pluggable **attention backend**).

You already know the *what* from the prerequisites. PagedAttention stores KV in fixed-size blocks reached through a per-request block table. FlashAttention-style kernels tile the computation so scores never touch HBM. A backend is the glue that feeds vLLM's block tables into one such kernel.

A backend in vLLM (`vllm/v1/attention/backend.py`) has three parts:

1. `AttentionBackend`: a class with no per-step state. It names itself (`get_name`) and declares what it supports: model dtypes, KV cache dtypes, kernel block sizes, head sizes, compute capability, MLA or not, sinks, sliding window. It also returns the other two classes.
2. `AttentionMetadataBuilder`: runs once per step for each KV cache group: a set of layers whose caches have the same shape and share one block table, for example all full-attention layers, with sliding-window layers in a second group. It turns the shared batch description into the tensors this kernel wants.
3. `AttentionImpl`: one instance per layer. Its `forward` method takes the layer's query, key and value, the KV cache and the metadata, and writes the result into an `output` tensor.

blocks.title: One decode step through an attention backend

nodes.label:
Metadata builder
(one per KV cache group)

scenes.caption: The scheduler says how many tokens each request runs this step. Nothing backend-specific has happened yet.
The runner flattens the batch into one token list and fills CommonAttentionMetadata: query_start_loc, seq_lens, block_table_tensor, slot_mapping. Every backend gets this same description.

The chosen backend's builder turns the shared description into its own metadata once per step, for example FlashAttention scheduler data or FlashInfer plans. This is the only per-step backend-specific setup.

Every attention layer reuses that one metadata object. Each layer first writes the new K and V into the paged cache at the slots in slot_mapping, then calls the kernel that reads the blocks back through the block table.

blocks.md:
The shared input, `CommonAttentionMetadata`, carries what any paged kernel needs. Its main fields are:

- `query_start_loc` with shape (batch + 1): where each request's new tokens start in the flattened token list.
- `seq_lens`: the total length of each request after this step (cached context plus new tokens).
- `num_reqs`, `num_actual_tokens`, `max_query_len`, `max_seq_len`.
- `block_table_tensor`: the per-request block tables from PagedAttention.
- `slot_mapping`: for each new token, the flat cache slot its K and V go into.

blocks.caption: A complete out-of-tree backend, part 1 of 3: declaration and builder, with names and signatures from vLLM main (commit 8d5e012). Not run inside vLLM here (no GPU); a CPU test with stub base classes ran parts 1 to 3 on lesson 4's batch and matched dense attention to 3.6e-7.
Part 2: the per-layer impl. The signatures match AttentionImpl in vllm/v1/attention/backend.py. The impl refuses sliding windows and FP8 caches rather than computing them wrongly.

blocks.code:
import torch

def write_kv(key, value, kv_cache, slot_mapping, head_size):
    # kv_cache: [num_blocks, H_kv, block_size, 2*D]; view as [num_blocks, block_size, H_kv, 2*D]
    k_cache, v_cache = kv_cache.transpose(1, 2).split(head_size, dim=-1)
    bs = kv_cache.shape[2]
    n = slot_mapping.shape[0]
    keep = slot_mapping >= 0                      # PAD_SLOT_ID = -1 rows are skipped
    s = slot_mapping[keep]
    k_cache[s // bs, s % bs] = key[:n][keep]
    v_cache[s // bs, s % bs] = value[:n][keep]

def paged_attention(query, kv_cache, qsl, seq_lens, block_table, scale, head_size, out):
    k_cache, v_cache = kv_cache.transpose(1, 2).split(head_size, dim=-1)
    bs = kv_cache.shape[2]
    g = query.shape[1] // kv_cache.shape[1]       # query heads per KV head (GQA)
    for r in range(len(seq_lens)):
        q0, q1, L = qsl[r], qsl[r + 1], seq_lens[r]
        if q1 == q0:
            continue                               # padded request: query length 0
        pos = torch.arange(L)
        blk = block_table[r, pos // bs]            # gather this request's pages
        k = k_cache[blk, pos % bs].repeat_interleave(g, dim=1)   # [L, H, D]
        v = v_cache[blk, pos % bs].repeat_interleave(g, dim=1)
        q = query[q0:q1]                           # [n, H, D]
        s = torch.einsum("nhd,lhd->hnl", q, k) * scale
        qpos = torch.arange(L - (q1 - q0), L)      # absolute positions of new tokens
        s = s.masked_fill(pos[None, None, :] > qpos[None, :, None], float("-inf"))
        out[q0:q1] = torch.einsum("hnl,lhd->nhd", s.softmax(-1), v)
    return out
blocks.caption: Part 3, ref_impl.py: the reference math in plain PyTorch. A token's K and V go to slot s, which is offset s mod B of block s // B; rows with slot -1 are padding. Each request then gathers its keys page by page and applies a causal mask. This part runs on a CPU; lesson 4 tests it.

blocks.md:
To use it, package the three parts as a plugin. A function listed under the `vllm.general_plugins` entry point imports the module, so `@register_backend` runs before the engine starts (vLLM's plugin system doc describes the entry point). Then start a small model with `--attention-backend CUSTOM` and compare greedy outputs against `FLASH_ATTN`.

Expect the same greedy tokens on most prompts, but exact agreement is not guaranteed: the two kernels add up the same terms in a different order, and one flipped low bit can change a greedy choice later on (floating-point addition is not associative).

Two details from the source are worth knowing. `build()` still takes `common_prefix_len`, but backend.py documents it as deprecated and always 0: there is no shared-prefix feature to implement. And `NEVER` has a consequence you can see in the startup log, covered in lesson 8.

blocks.md:
Two builder class attributes come back in later lessons. `reorder_batch_threshold` is the longest query the builder still treats as a decode (the runner already sorts decodes to the front). `_cudagraph_support` says which batches this backend can run inside a captured CUDA graph.

The registry is `AttentionBackendEnum` in `vllm/v1/attention/backends/registry.py`. Each member's value is a class path, for example `FLASH_ATTN`, `FLASHINFER`, `TRITON_ATTN`, `FLEX_ATTENTION`, `FLASHMLA`, `CUTLASS_MLA`, `FLASHINFER_MLA`, `TRITON_MLA`, `FLASH_ATTN_MLA`, `ROCM_ATTN`, `CPU_ATTN` and `CPU_MLA`. A `CUSTOM` placeholder lets plugins register their own. `ROCM_ATTN` runs on ROCm, AMD's GPU software platform, and `FLEX_ATTENTION` uses PyTorch's FlexAttention, which compiles an attention variant written as a small Python scoring function into a kernel.

A backend is mostly a *declaration*: what it supports, plus two factories. Selection, batching, KV layout and CUDA graph capture are all driven by those declarations, so a backend never needs to know about the scheduler.

blocks.question: A model has 32 attention layers that all use the same backend and one KV cache group. In one engine step, how many times does that backend's metadata builder run `build()`?
options: Once, and all 32 layers reuse the result
32 times, once per layer, because each layer has its own KV cache
Once per request in the batch
Zero times on decode steps, because decode metadata is cached
blocks.explain: The builder runs once per step per KV cache group, and the layers in that group share the metadata object. Per-layer work happens in `AttentionImpl.forward`. That is why `forward` must stay cheap on the CPU.

blocks.question: Which piece declares that a backend needs compute capability 8.0 or higher?
options: The `AttentionImpl` instance, by checking the GPU inside `forward`
The metadata builder, by raising during `build()`
The `AttentionBackend` class, through `supports_compute_capability`, which selection calls before anything runs
The scheduler, which skips requests on unsupported GPUs
blocks.explain: Capabilities live on the backend class so they can be checked at startup. `validate_configuration` calls `supports_compute_capability` along with the head size, dtype, KV dtype and block size checks.

blocks.question: Your reference backend declares `_cudagraph_support = AttentionCGSupport.NEVER` and you start it with the default `-O2`. What happens?
options: Startup fails, because FULL_AND_PIECEWISE needs at least UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE
vLLM captures full graphs anyway and replays them with stale Python lists
vLLM silently picks FLASH_ATTN instead
vLLM logs a warning and falls back to PIECEWISE graphs, so attention runs eagerly while the other pieces still replay as graphs
blocks.explain: The default mode only asks for full graphs on decode batches, and the resolver downgrades that to PIECEWISE when support is NEVER and attention is a splitting op. Only modes that ask for full graphs on mixed batches raise an error with NEVER. Selection never swaps a backend you named.

lessons.title: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation

blocks.md: At startup each attention layer calls `get_attn_backend` in `vllm/v1/attention/selector.py`. That function packs the layer's facts into an `AttentionSelectorConfig`: head size, model dtype, KV cache dtype, block size (only if you pinned `--block-size`), MLA or not, sinks, sparse (attention that reads only a chosen subset of earlier tokens, as in DeepSeek-V3.2), sliding window, and more. The platform's `get_attn_backend_cls` then picks a class.

On CUDA the rule (`vllm/platforms/cuda.py`) is short:

1. If you named a backend, validate only that one. If it fails, raise `ValueError` with the reasons. There is no silent fallback.
2. Otherwise take the priority list for this GPU and attention type. Run `validate_configuration` on every entry and keep the valid ones.
3. Pick the valid backend with the best priority. Log the full list of valid candidates.
4. If nothing is valid, raise an error that lists every backend and why it failed.

blocks.title: Walking the CUDA priority list (standard attention)

nodes.label:
Selector config
head size, dtypes, block size

scenes.caption: On any GPU that is not compute capability 10.x, the standard list is FLASH_ATTN, FLASHINFER, TRITON_ATTN, FLEX_ATTENTION, TURBOQUANT. TURBOQUANT serves vLLM's TurboQuant compressed KV formats. Each entry is checked against the same config.
H100 (compute capability 9.0), BF16 model, head size 128, block size not pinned. FLASH_ATTN validates, and on Hopper it defaults to FlashAttention-3. Priority 1 wins.

T4 (compute capability 7.5, Turing), FP16 model. FLASH_ATTN needs capability 8.0 or higher, and FLASHINFER is currently limited to 8.0 through 12.1. TRITON_ATTN accepts any capability and head sizes of 32 or more, so it wins.

On compute capability 10.x (data-center Blackwell) with causal attention, the list puts FLASHINFER first (its kernels from TensorRT-LLM, NVIDIA's inference library), then FLASH_ATTN. If you set non-causal attention, FLASH_ATTN goes back to the front.
Back on the T4: --attention-backend FLASHINFER skips the list. Only FLASHINFER is validated, it fails the capability check, and startup stops with a ValueError naming the reason.

blocks.md:
MLA models (`use_mla=True`) use separate lists. On compute capability 10.x the dense part (backends that attend to every earlier token) starts `FLASHINFER_MLA`, `TOKENSPEED_MLA`, `CUTLASS_MLA`, `FLASH_ATTN_MLA`, `FLASHMLA`, `TRITON_MLA`. On other capabilities, 9.x included, it starts `FLASH_ATTN_MLA`, `FLASHMLA`, `FLASHINFER_MLA`, `TRITON_MLA`. On 12.x (consumer Blackwell, such as RTX 50-series cards) the list is `TRITON_MLA` and then a sparse backend. Sparse MLA entries come after the dense ones, and their order depends on the KV dtype and head count.

MLA has two halves. The backend above handles decode. Prefill is chosen separately (`-ac.mla_prefill_backend`, with options such as `FLASH_ATTN`, `FLASHINFER` and `TRTLLM_RAGGED`, a TensorRT-LLM kernel for ragged batches, meaning variable-length sequences packed without padding), automatically by default.

Other platforms have their own logic. On CPU, standard attention always gets `CPU_ATTN`. MLA gets `AMX_MLA` when the x86 CPU has AMX (Advanced Matrix Extensions, Intel's on-chip matrix-multiply tile units), and `CPU_MLA` otherwise.

blocks.md: Older guides set the `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND` environment variable. It existed in `vllm/envs.py` up to the v0.14 release and is gone from main. Use `--attention-backend` or `--attention-config` (`-ac`). `AttentionConfig.backend_per_kind` can also set a backend per KV cache group kind, for example a different one for sliding-window MLA layers.

Two smaller rules matter in practice. FlashAttention picks its version by GPU: FA3 (FlashAttention-3) on compute capability 9.x, FA4 (FlashAttention-4) on 10.x when it is installed, and FA2 (FlashAttention-2) otherwise. You can override this with `flash_attn_version`. And if you pin `--block-size` without pinning a backend, a higher-priority backend may be rejected only because of the block size. vLLM then logs a warning that `--block-size` precluded those backends and suggests removing the flag.

Selection picks the first *valid* backend, not the fastest one for your workload. To check, pin two backends on the same model and time them with `vllm bench latency`, which accepts every engine flag, `--attention-backend` included. Set `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG` to see the selector's line *Using X attention backend out of potential backends: [...]*, which lists every candidate that passed validation.

Run two shapes. A decode-heavy run (short prompts, long outputs) spends nearly all its steps in single-token decode, so latency per output token approximates the average decode step (TPOT, not ITL): the decode kernel and whether the backend can replay full CUDA graphs (lesson 8). It times whole batches; ITL percentiles need `vllm bench serve`. A prefill-heavy run (long prompts, one output token) measures the prefill kernel, which sets time to first token (TTFT). A backend can win one and lose the other. For percentiles under load and how to avoid fooling yourself, see lesson 3 of *LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management*.

blocks.md: Automatic selection takes the first backend in the platform's priority list that passes `validate_configuration`. Explicit selection validates one backend and fails loudly. Neither path guesses.

blocks.question: On an A100 (compute capability 8.0) you start a BF16 model with `--attention-backend FLASHMLA`. The model is not MLA. What happens?
options: vLLM ignores the flag and uses FLASH_ATTN, the first valid entry
Startup fails with a ValueError listing reasons such as compute capability not supported and non-MLA not supported
FLASHMLA runs, but more slowly than FLASH_ATTN
vLLM switches to TRITON_MLA because it accepts any GPU
blocks.explain: An explicit backend is validated alone. FLASHMLA reports `is_mla()` as true and accepts only capability 9.x or 10.x, so `validate_configuration` returns reasons and `get_attn_backend_cls` raises. The design doc shows this same error format.

blocks.question: On a B200 serving a DeepSeek-style MLA model you pinned `--block-size 16`. The log warns that block size 16 precluded the higher-priority backends FLASHINFER_MLA, CUTLASS_MLA and FLASHMLA. FLASHINFER_MLA supports block sizes 32 and 64. What fixes it?
options: Keep the flag and add `--attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA`
Set `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASHINFER_MLA`
Raise `--gpu-memory-utilization` so the larger blocks fit
Remove `--block-size` (or pin 32 or 64), so FLASHINFER_MLA passes validation and wins on priority
blocks.explain: A pinned block size goes into the selector config, and `supports_block_size` rejects 16 because it is not a multiple of 32 or 64. Forcing the backend while keeping 16 fails validation with a ValueError. The environment variable no longer exists. Removing the pin lets vLLM use the backend's preferred size.

lessons.title: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass

blocks.md: vLLM V1 (the rewritten engine whose code lives under `vllm/v1`) has no separate prefill and decode steps. Each step the scheduler hands out a token budget (at most `max_num_batched_tokens` new tokens per step), and one forward pass can mix requests that decode one token, requests that continue a chunked prefill (a long prompt processed one slice per step, so decodes are not stalled behind it), and brand-new prompts. The runner flattens all their new tokens into one list. `query_start_loc` marks where each request's tokens begin, and `seq_lens` holds each request's total length after this step.

Our running example has five requests:

- A, C and E are decoding: their prompts are done (40, 17 and 60 tokens computed) and each runs 1 token.
- D is a chunked prefill: 32 of its 50 prompt tokens are cached, and it runs 5 more.
- B is new: 0 tokens computed, and it runs its whole 6-token prompt.

That is 14 tokens in total, listed here as A, B, C, D, E; the runner sorts them before any backend sees them.

Why only 5 for D? Say the budget is `max_num_batched_tokens = 14` in this toy (real budgets are thousands of tokens; when later lessons pad this step for a CUDA graph, they assume such a default server). The scheduler first serves running requests (A, C, E: 1 token each), then waiting ones in order. B takes its whole 6-token prompt. D is new too, but its first 32 prompt tokens hit the prefix cache (two full 16-token blocks), so 18 need computing and the 5 left in the budget become this step's chunk. The other 13 wait for the next step.

blocks.title: Sorting a mixed batch: decodes first

scenes.caption: The five requests in listed order, flattened into 14 tokens: query_start_loc would be [0, 1, 7, 8, 13, 14]. No backend sees this order on main, because the runner sorts every batch first.
sort_batch_req_ids keys each request by: has no draft tokens, query length differs from the decode length (1 here), then query length. A, C and E run exactly 1 token; D runs 5 and B runs 6.

Sorted: the three decodes first, then the rest by ascending query length, so D (5) comes before B (6). This happens for every backend, whatever its reorder_batch_threshold. Decodes now occupy tokens 0 to 2.
The metadata now reads query_start_loc = [0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 14] and seq_lens = [41, 18, 61, 37, 6]. One integer, num_decode_tokens = 3, splits the batch for backends that need two kernels.

blocks.md: On vLLM main the GPU model runner (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py`) sorts every batch the same way, whatever the backends declare. `sort_batch_req_ids` puts requests that verify draft tokens first, then requests whose query length equals the decode length (1 without speculative decoding), then the rest by ascending query length. A builder's `reorder_batch_threshold` no longer triggers a reorder: the builder passes it to `split_decodes_and_prefills` as the longest query that still counts as a decode. That function finds the boundary, and with `require_uniform` set, it also needs every decode to have the same length.

Backends then go different ways:

- **FLASH_ATTN** sets no threshold. It makes one variable-length kernel call over all 14 tokens, with `cu_seqlens_q = query_start_loc` (cumulative query lengths, which are exactly the start offsets), `seqused_k = seq_lens` (how many cached key positions each request reads) and the block table. Each query row attends causally to its own request's pages.
- **FLASHINFER** uses threshold 1. It runs a decode kernel on the first 3 rows of `output` (the decodes) and a prefill kernel on the remaining 11.

**MLA backends** split into two math paths. Decode tokens go through `forward_mqa`, which works on the 576-wide compressed latent like multi-query attention, where all query heads share one key-value head. The 576 is DeepSeek-V3's 512-wide latent plus its 64-wide rotary key part. Instead of expanding the latent into keys, each query is first multiplied by the matrix that would have expanded it, so every head can score directly against the one shared latent. Prefill tokens go through `forward_mha`, which first expands the latent into per-head K and V. `FLASHMLA` uses threshold 128 with uniform decodes. `FLASH_ATTN_MLA` uses threshold 512 and accepts mixed lengths, so short prefills take the decode path.

blocks.tex: s_{h,t} = q_h^{\top} k_{h,t} = q_h^{\top}\big(W^{UK}_h c_t\big) = \big((W^{UK}_h)^{\top} q_h\big)^{\top} c_t
blocks.caption: Score of head h against cached token t, ignoring the 64-wide rotary part. W^UK_h is 128 x 512 in DeepSeek-V3. Multiplying the query by its transpose once gives a 512-wide query that dots directly with the cached latent c_t.

blocks.md:
Count the work for one decode token of one DeepSeek-V3 layer (128 heads; per head 128 + 64 for keys, 128 for values; latent 512) at 4,096 cached tokens. Expanding first costs $2 \cdot 512 \cdot 128 \cdot (128 + 128) \approx 33.6$ million FLOPs *per cached token* to rebuild K and V, about $1.38 \times 10^{11}$ in total. Absorbing costs the same 33.6 million once per *query* (project q, and later project the 512-wide output back to values), then $2 \cdot 576 + 2 \cdot 512 = 2{,}176$ FLOPs per cached token per head: about $1.17 \times 10^{9}$, 117 times less. It reads 1,152 bytes per cached token in BF16 instead of the 81,920 that expanded K and V would take.

Prefill flips this. With 4,096 queries over 4,096 keys the up-projection is shared by all queries, and each query-key pair costs 640 FLOPs per head in the expanded form ($2 \cdot 192 + 2 \cdot 128$) against 2,176 in the latent form: $1.51 \times 10^{12}$ versus $4.81 \times 10^{12}$. Hence MQA form for decode, MHA form for prefill.

blocks.prompt: Same 14-token batch, now on a DeepSeek-style MLA model with FLASH_ATTN_MLA (threshold 512, variable-length decode). How many tokens go to the decode path?
blocks.reveal:
All **14**. In `split_decodes_and_prefills`, `max_query_len` is 6, which is at most 512, and uniformity is not required, so every request counts as a decode, even B's fresh prompt. The source says this on purpose: *process small prefills with decode pathway*.

With FLASHMLA (threshold 128, uniform), A, C and E have length 1, while D (5) and B (6) do not match, so the split is 3 decode tokens and 11 prefill tokens.

blocks.title: Where the 14 tokens go, by backend

scenes.caption: FLASH_ATTN: one kernel handles decodes and prefills together, so no split is needed.
FLASHINFER (threshold 1): the 3 single-token decodes go to the decode kernel, and D's 5 plus B's 6 go to the prefill kernel.
FLASHMLA (threshold 128, uniform decodes): D and B have lengths 5 and 6, not 1, so the split matches FlashInfer.
FLASH_ATTN_MLA (threshold 512, variable length): the whole batch takes the latent-space MQA path.

blocks.md: Writing new K and V uses `slot_mapping`. For a token at position $p$ in a request with block table $T$ and block size $B$:

blocks.caption: Example: T = [7, 1, 3] and B = 16. Position 37 is in logical block 2 at offset 5, so its slot is 3 x 16 + 5 = 53. Position 16 maps to slot 16 and position 0 to slot 112. Padded token rows get PAD_SLOT_ID = -1, so no real slot is written.

blocks.md: A mixed batch is one flat list of tokens plus offsets, sorted decodes first by the runner. Backends with one variable-length kernel do not care about the order. Backends with separate decode and prefill kernels split it with one index.

blocks.question: Request D has 32 of its 50 prompt tokens computed and runs 5 tokens; B is a fresh 6-token prompt; A, C and E decode 1 token each. Where does the runner's sort put D?
options: After the three decodes and before B, because the rest are ordered by query length (5 < 6)
With the decodes, since it already has context
At the very end, after B, because its prompt is unfinished
Nowhere special: FLASH_ATTN sets no threshold, so the batch is not sorted
blocks.explain: sort_batch_req_ids puts requests whose query length equals the decode length (1) first, then orders the rest by query length. Context does not enter the key, so D (5) precedes B (6); had B been a 3-token prompt, B would have come first. The sort runs for every backend.

blocks.question: A model mixes a backend whose builder reports `reorder_batch_threshold = 1` with one that reports `None`. Is the batch sorted decodes first?
options: No, because None disables reordering for everyone
Yes, but each backend gets its own differently ordered copy of the batch
Yes: the runner sorts every batch decode-first whatever the thresholds say; the threshold only tells each builder where its decodes end
Only on steps that contain no prefills
blocks.explain: On main, sort_batch_req_ids in the GPU model runner orders every batch, and one order is shared by all layers. reorder_batch_threshold is read only by builders, which pass it to split_decodes_and_prefills as the decode cutoff. Backends with one varlen kernel, such as FLASH_ATTN, accept any order.

lessons.title: Inside FLASH_ATTN's forward: from slot_mapping to one kernel call

blocks.md:
Lesson 3 ended with a batch description. Now watch one layer use it. Start with request D: after this step it has 37 tokens, and positions 32 to 36 are new. Before attention can run, their keys and values must sit in the paged cache. Then one kernel call reads all 37 back through D's block table.

The model's `Attention` layer makes those two calls, both PyTorch custom ops. `unified_kv_cache_update` runs the impl's `do_kv_cache_update`, and `unified_attention_with_output` runs its `forward`. Backends that set `forward_includes_kv_cache_update = False`, as FLASH_ATTN, TRITON_ATTN and FLASHINFER do, are driven this way. The first op returns an empty dummy tensor that the second takes as an argument, so torch.compile sees a data dependency and cannot reorder them.

Shapes for one Llama-3-8B layer (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head size 128, BF16, block size 16) and the 14-token batch. The runner has already sorted the batch (lesson 3), so the rows are in order A, C, E, D, B.

- `query`: [16, 32, 128]. `key` and `value`: [16, 8, 128]. `output`: [16, 32, 128]. The step is padded to 16 rows for a CUDA graph (lesson 8): 14 real rows (`num_actual_tokens` = 14) plus 2 padding rows.
- `kv_cache` for this layer: [num_blocks, 8, 16, 256], blocks by KV heads by tokens by K and V side by side.
- `kv_cache.transpose(1, 2).split(128, dim=-1)` gives `key_cache` and `value_cache`, each [num_blocks, 16, 8, 128]. These are views: nothing is copied.

Give the requests toy block tables: A [2, 9, 5], B [11], C [4, 12], D [7, 1, 3] (lesson 3's slot example), E [6, 10, 8, 13]. The builder mostly passes fields through:

- `cu_seqlens_q` = `query_start_loc` = [0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 14]
- `seqused_k` = `seq_lens` = [41, 18, 61, 37, 6]; `max_seqlen_q` = 6, `max_seqlen_k` = 61
- `block_table`: int32, shape [5, width], unused entries 0
- `slot_mapping` = [88, 193, 220, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 176, 177, 178, 179, 180, 181]

On FA3 the builder also calls `get_scheduler_metadata` ahead of time: FA3 plans how to split the work across the GPU before the launch, and with full CUDA graphs that plan is copied into a persistent buffer.

blocks.title: The cache write: 14 tokens, 14 slots, 2 padded rows skipped

scenes.caption: Each new token's slot is T[p // 16] x 16 + p mod 16 for its request's table T. With default graph sizes (lesson 8) the step pads to 16 rows, so rows 14 and 15 carry PAD_SLOT_ID = -1.

reshape_and_cache_flash runs one thread block per row. D's rows 3 to 7 hold slots 48 to 52: block 48 // 16 = 3, offsets 0 to 4. Its K and V land there, and the block's last 11 offsets stay free for later tokens.

Rows 14 and 15: the kernel reads slot -1 and returns at once (the source comment: slot_idx can be -1 if the token is padded). Padding never touches the cache. All 14 real tokens were written, as the CPU run below confirms.

blocks.title: One layer through FLASH_ATTN
blocks.code:
# Attention.forward for one layer (simplified)
q = q.view(-1, 32, 128)
k = k.view(-1, 8, 128)
v = v.view(-1, 8, 128)
dep = unified_kv_cache_update(k, v, layer_name)
unified_attention_with_output(q, k, v, out, layer_name, dep)

# op 1 calls FlashAttentionImpl.do_kv_cache_update
k_cache, v_cache = kv_cache.transpose(1, 2).split(128, dim=-1)
reshape_and_cache_flash(k, v, k_cache, v_cache, slot_mapping,
                        kv_cache_dtype, layer._k_scale, layer._v_scale)

# op 2 calls FlashAttentionImpl.forward
k_cache, v_cache = kv_cache.transpose(1, 2).split(128, dim=-1)
m = attn_metadata
flash_attn_varlen_func(
    q=q[:m.num_actual_tokens], k=k_cache, v=v_cache,
    out=out[:m.num_actual_tokens],
    cu_seqlens_q=m.query_start_loc, max_seqlen_q=m.max_query_len,
    seqused_k=m.seq_lens, max_seqlen_k=m.max_seq_len,
    block_table=m.block_table, softmax_scale=self.scale,
    causal=m.causal, window_size=self.sliding_window,
    scheduler_metadata=m.scheduler_metadata,
    q_descale=q_descale, k_descale=k_descale, v_descale=v_descale,
    s_aux=self.sinks, fa_version=self.vllm_flash_attn_version)

scenes.caption: The layer reshapes its projections into heads. GQA shows in the shapes: 32 query heads, 8 key and value heads. The 16 rows are the 14 real tokens plus 2 graph-padding rows.
Op 1 first. Its empty result dep is passed into op 2, which pins the order under torch.compile.
Inside op 1: split the layer's cache into K and V views, then scatter each new row to its slot.
scenes.output: D's positions 32 to 36 land in block 3, offsets 0 to 4 (slots 48 to 52). With a BF16 cache, kv_cache_dtype is auto and the scales are unused.

scenes.caption: Inside op 2: the same two views. The kernel gets the cache, not the new key and value tensors.
The variable-length metadata. Query row i belongs to the request r with cu_seqlens_q[r] <= i < cu_seqlens_q[r+1], and that request reads seqused_k[r] keys.
Paging, scale and masking. Keys are found through block_table; the scale is 1 / sqrt(128); (-1, -1) means no window.
FA3 plan, FP8 descales and sinks. With a BF16 cache and no sinks these carry nothing; lesson 6 covers FP8 and the text below covers sinks.

blocks.md:
How does one launch serve five requests? Row 4 of `q` is D's second new token. Since 3 <= 4 < 8 it belongs to request index 3, which is D: it has 37 keys and 5 new tokens, so the row sits at position 37 - 5 + 1 = 33. Causal masking lets it see positions 0 to 33, which the kernel reads page by page through `block_table[3]`.

Sliding windows travel the same way. The impl stores `(W - 1, 0)`, FlashAttention's left and right reach, and `(-1, -1)` when there is no window. Notice what is *not* passed: `key` and `value`. FLASH_ATTN reads every key, including this step's, from the cache, which is why the write must come first.

blocks.caption: Real output of a CPU model of this step: the reference write_kv and paged_attention from lesson 1, float32, 4 query heads, 2 KV heads, head size 8, the block tables above, two padded rows. Paged attention matches dense causal attention per request to 3.6e-7. Swapping the order breaks every row.

blocks.prompt: In the swapped run the kernel ran before the cache write. B's rows (8 to 13) are off by up to 2.24, but A's row only by 0.016. Why the difference?
blocks.reveal: Each row loses its own request's *new* keys and instead reads whatever the unwritten slots hold (zeros in this toy; stale data from a freed block on a real GPU). A has 40 correct cached keys and only 1 missing, so the damage is diluted. B is a fresh prompt: **all** of its keys are new, so every one of its rows attends to garbage. Small errors are still errors: greedy decoding would drift.

blocks.md:
**Sinks.** A model with attention sinks such as gpt-oss passes one learned value per query head as `s_aux`. FLASH_ATTN accepts this only on FlashAttention 3 or 4 (`flash_attn_supports_sinks`), so on an A100, which runs FA2, the backend fails validation for that model. FLASHINFER supports sinks only through its TensorRT-LLM kernels on compute capability 9.0, 10.x and 12.x, so it fails too. TRITON_ATTN declares sink support everywhere and is selected.

**A second implementation of the same contract.** `TritonAttentionImpl` writes the cache with its own Triton kernel and then calls `unified_attention` with the same `cu_seqlens_q`, `seqused_k`, `max_seqlen_q`, `max_seqlen_k`, `block_table`, window and sinks. Nothing upstream changes: the metadata contract is the interface.

Triton does choose between two launches. Its 2D kernel gives each program a block of query rows for one KV head. When a batch has too few query blocks to fill the GPU, the 3D kernel also splits every request's keys into 16 segments, keeps each segment's running max and sum in scratch buffers that the builder allocated up front, and merges them afterwards: the split-KV idea from the Flash-Decoding part of the *FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4* course.

The rule, with default settings: use 3D when every query is at most 8 tokens, `num_seqs` x ceil(`max_seqlen_q` / BLOCK_Q) is at most 128 / `num_kv_heads`, and the scratch buffers have a row per query token. For Llama-3-8B the limit is 16 (also the scratch rows without speculative decoding), and BLOCK_Q = 16 rows / 4 query heads per KV head = 4 tokens. Our batch has 5 x ceil(6 / 4) = 10 query blocks and 14 tokens, so it takes the 3D path.

vLLM deleted its original PagedAttention CUDA kernel (`paged_attention_v1`/`v2`) in July 2026 (PR #47361). Older posts that call it vLLM's attention kernel describe history. On main, every backend reads pages inside its own kernel through `block_table`. The *PagedAttention and prefix caching* course covers how that kernel worked.

Per layer, a backend does two things in a fixed order: scatter this step's K and V to `slot_mapping`, then run one variable-length kernel that reads every key, old and new, from the paged cache. The metadata (`cu_seqlens_q`, `seqused_k`, `block_table`) is the whole contract between them.

blocks.question: A contributor moves `reshape_and_cache_flash` to run after `flash_attn_varlen_func` in a FLASH_ATTN-style backend. What breaks?
options: Only padded rows, because PAD_SLOT_ID is now checked too late
Nothing, because the kernel receives `key` and `value` directly and only reads the cache for older tokens
Every new token attends to unwritten slots instead of this step's keys, so outputs are wrong, worst for fresh prompts
The cache switches from token-major to head-major byte order
blocks.explain: The kernel's k and v arguments are the paged cache views. Keys for positions computed this step exist only after the write, so a query that should see itself and the earlier tokens of its chunk reads empty or stale slots instead. A fresh prompt has no correct keys at all.

blocks.question: Row 6 of the 14-token batch belongs to which request, and at which absolute position?
options: D, position 35
D, position 6
E, position 60
D, position 36
blocks.explain: cu_seqlens_q = [0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 14], and 3 <= 6 < 8, so it is request 3, D. D's 5 new tokens start at 37 - 5 = 32, and row 6 is D's fourth new row (offset 3), so its position is 35 and its slot is 3 x 16 + 3 = 51.

lessons.title: KV cache layout and block sizes per backend

blocks.md:
Every backend reads the same paged cache, but kernels care about *byte order* inside it. vLLM describes a layer's page logically as $[B, H, N, C]$: blocks, KV head slots, tokens in the block, and content. $C$ is the bytes of one head's key and value for one token: $(D_k + D_v)$ times the dtype size, where $D_k$ and $D_v$ are the key and value head dimensions (128 each in the example below). Stacking layers adds $L$, giving $[L, B, H, N, C]$.

FlashAttention views a layer as a tensor whose dimensions are blocks, KV heads, tokens per block, and 2 times the head size. It transposes heads and tokens, then splits the last dimension into K and V.

blocks.caption: H is KV heads, N is block size in tokens, s is bytes per element. A Llama-3-8B-shaped layer (8 KV heads, head size 128, BF16) with N = 16 gives 8 × 16 × (128 + 128) × 2 = 65,536 bytes per page, or 4,096 bytes per token per layer and 131,072 bytes per token over 32 layers.

blocks.md: MLA changes the content, not the scheme. vLLM builds the MLA spec with one KV head whose size is the latent width (`kv_lora_rank`, the rank of MLA's low-rank compression) plus the rotary key width (`qk_rope_head_dim`), and no separate V, because the kernels read values from the same latent. With DeepSeek-V3's 512 + 64 that is 576 elements, or 1,152 bytes per token per layer in BF16, which is 3.56 times less than the GQA example. FLASHMLA requires 64-token blocks, so one page is 73,728 bytes.

The physical order is a `KVCacheLayout`, a permutation of $[L, B, H, N, C]$: `LBHNC`, `LBNHC`, `LHBNC`, `BLHNC`, `BLNHC`, `BHLNC`. Backends declare what their kernels accept with `supported_kv_cache_layouts()`:

- FLASH_ATTN declares nothing, so any layout works.
- FLASHINFER on compute capability 10.x wants head-major blocks (`LBHNC` or `BLHNC`) for the trtllm-gen kernels (kernels generated by NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM project).
- FLEX_ATTENTION wants `LBNHC`.
- CPU_ATTN wants `LBHNC`.

The engine core resolves **one** layout for the whole model. It intersects all declarations and prefers the layout most backends list first. If nobody declares, the default order is `LBNHC`, `LBHNC`, `BLNHC`, `BLHNC`, `BHLNC`, `LHBNC`. `VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT` can force a choice, but it must be one of the candidates. The legacy names `NHD` and `HND` (N tokens, H heads, D head dimension) alias `LBNHC` and `LBHNC`.

blocks.title: Same block, two byte orders (2 heads, 3 tokens)

scenes.caption: Each cell holds C bytes: one head's K and V for one token. Both rows store the same 6 cells, in different orders.
Head-major (LBHNC): all tokens of head 0 are contiguous, which suits kernels that stream one head at a time. In LBNHC the same cells are strided by the number of heads.
Token-major (LBNHC): all heads of token 1 sit side by side, so writing one new token's K and V touches one contiguous run.

The L and B axes nest outside a block. With L outer, each layer's cache is one contiguous tensor. With B outer, block 0 of every layer is adjacent, so a whole block moves as one run, which helps KV transfer (copying a request's cache to another server).

blocks.md:
Block size is also negotiated. Each backend lists kernel block sizes with `get_supported_kernel_block_sizes`:

- FLASH_ATTN, TRITON_ATTN, FLEX_ATTENTION and TRITON_MLA: multiples of 16.
- FLASHINFER: 16, 32 or 64, plus larger pages on Blackwell when its TRTLLM path applies.
- FLASHINFER_MLA: 32 or 64. FLASHMLA: 64. CUTLASS_MLA: 128. CPU_ATTN: multiples of 32.

The default is 16. If you did not pin `--block-size`, vLLM asks the backend for its preferred size. That is the default when the backend accepts it, and otherwise the smallest size the backend supports. With several backends, it uses the smallest size that all of them accept.

The block table itself is small but not free. Each row is `int32` with $\lceil L / B \rceil$ entries, where $L$ is `max_model_len`, rounded up so a row covers a multiple of 128 tokens. For 32,768 tokens and $B = 16$ that is 2,048 entries, 8 KiB per request and 2 MiB for 256 requests. With $B = 64$ it is 512 entries, or 512 KiB in total. For a 1,000-token limit and $B = 16$, the 63 entries round up to 64.

scenes.caption: int32 entries, rows padded to cover a multiple of 128 tokens. Larger blocks shrink the table, and longer contexts grow it linearly.

blocks.md: A KV cache layout is chosen once for the whole model, not per layer. If two backends in one model share no layout, startup fails with *No KV cache layout satisfies every supported set* rather than converting at runtime.

blocks.question: You serve an MLA model on Hopper with `--attention-backend FLASHMLA`, and you never passed `--block-size`. What block size does the KV cache use?
options: 16, the CacheConfig default, and FlashMLA pads each block
128, the largest size any MLA backend uses
It depends on max_model_len
64, because with no pinned size vLLM takes the backend's preferred size and FLASHMLA supports only 64
blocks.explain: Unpinned block sizes give way to the backend. `get_preferred_block_size` returns the default if it is supported and otherwise the smallest supported size, and FLASHMLA lists only 64. Had you pinned 16, FLASHMLA would have been rejected during selection.

blocks.question: Which layout puts every KV head of one token next to each other inside a block?
options: LBHNC
LBNHC
LHBNC
BHLNC
blocks.explain: In LBNHC the order inside a block is N, then H, then C, so for a fixed token all heads are adjacent. LBHNC and BHLNC keep each head's tokens together instead, and LHBNC moves heads outside the block.

lessons.title: FP8 KV caches inside the backends: scales, kernels, support

blocks.md:
A tiny example first. A key element worth 2.9 is written to an FP8 cache with scale 1.0: it becomes the E4M3 number 3.0, one byte instead of two. When the kernel reads it back, it multiplies by the same scale and computes with 3.0.

E4M3 (4 exponent and 3 mantissa bits, largest value 448) appeared in lesson 5 of *FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4*. E5M2 moves one bit from the mantissa to the exponent, so it reaches 57,344 with coarser steps. The optional courses *FP8 and FP4 training* and *KV cache compression and quantization* (lesson 4) cover the formats and calibration in depth. This lesson stays inside the backend: where the scales live, which kernel applies them, and why a backend can refuse an FP8 cache.

`--kv-cache-dtype` takes `auto` (the model's dtype), `fp8`, `fp8_e4m3` or `fp8_e5m2`, plus newer formats outside this course. On CUDA, `fp8` means E4M3: the cache kernels treat the two names the same. Each backend lists what it accepts in `supported_kv_cache_dtypes`, and `validate_configuration` rejects a backend whose list lacks your choice. FLASH_ATTN adds a runtime check: an FP8 cache needs FA3 on compute capability 9.x or FA4 on 10.x (FA4 on 9.x only at head size 512), and E5M2 is never supported.

blocks.title: Which backends accept which FP8 KV cache (source on main)

scenes.caption: 1 means supported. The MLA row also covers TRITON_MLA and FLASHINFER_MLA, which list fp8 and fp8_e4m3 only. FLASH_ATTN_MLA and FLEX_ATTENTION accept no FP8 cache at all.
E5M2: FLASHINFER, TRITON_ATTN and CPU_ATTN list it, and FLASH_ATTN never accepts it. On an H100, --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e5m2 therefore makes automatic selection skip to FLASHINFER.
Per-head scales: only FLASH_ATTN on FA3 or newer reports supports_per_head_quant_scales, matching the docs, which also say they need llm-compressor calibration.

blocks.md:
**Where the scales live.** Every `Attention` layer carries `_q_scale`, `_k_scale` and `_v_scale` tensors. A calibrated checkpoint loads them; otherwise vLLM fills them with 1.0 after loading (`set_default_quant_scales`). A per-tensor scale has shape [1]. Per-head scales have shape [num_kv_heads] for K and V and [num_heads] for Q.

**Write path.** `do_kv_cache_update` passes `kv_cache_dtype`, `layer._k_scale` and `layer._v_scale` to `reshape_and_cache_flash`. The CUDA conversion stores x / scale, saturated to the largest finite FP8 value (`__NV_SATFINITE`). The comment in `quant_utils.cuh` states the contract: quantize HP / scale, dequantize FP8 x scale. The cache memory is raw bytes; `forward` views it as the platform's FP8 dtype.

**Read path.** FlashAttention wants descale tensors of shape (num_sequences, num_kv_heads), here (5, 8). The impl builds them with `layer._k_scale.expand((5, 8))`, a view with stride 0, so nothing is copied. On FA4 a per-tensor scale of exactly 1.0 is passed as `None` instead, because FA4 reads a missing descale as 1.0 and would otherwise copy the expanded views, three copy kernels per layer per step.

**Queries.** The docs note that with FA3 and an FP8 cache, attention itself runs in FP8, with queries quantized too. The layer does this before the custom op: if the impl says `supports_quant_query_input`, it quantizes `query` with `_q_scale`, and the kernel gets `q_descale`. TRITON_ATTN passes `q_descale` only when the query already arrives in FP8.

blocks.title: Five key values through E4M3 and E5M2 (computed)

scenes.caption: Toy values for one key row, including an outlier of 600 in one channel. Each will be stored as x / scale in one byte and read back times the scale.
E4M3 with the default scale 1.0: 600 saturates to 448 (25.3% error) and 0.003 rounds to 0.0039 (30.2%), near E4M3's smallest step of 0.00195. Middle values lose 1 to 5%.
A calibrated scale of 600 / 448 = 1.339 maps the largest value to 448: 600 comes back exact, 0.003 now has 12.8% error, the rest stay within 4%.
E5M2 with scale 1.0 does not clip: 600 becomes 640 (6.7%), and its wider exponent keeps 0.003 at 2.3%. The price is one fewer mantissa bit for every value.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np, ml_dtypes      # pip install numpy ml_dtypes

def fp8_roundtrip(x, scale, dt, maxv):   # store sat(x / scale), read back * scale
    y = np.clip(np.asarray(x, np.float32) / scale, -maxv, maxv)
    return y.astype(dt).astype(np.float32) * scale

k = np.array([0.003, 0.37, 2.9, 21.0, 600.0], np.float32)
for dt, maxv, name in ((ml_dtypes.float8_e4m3fn, 448.0, "e4m3"),
                       (ml_dtypes.float8_e5m2, 57344.0, "e5m2")):
    for scale in (1.0, float(np.abs(k).max() / maxv)):
        d = fp8_roundtrip(k, scale, dt, maxv)
        err = [round(float(e), 1) for e in 100 * np.abs(d - k) / k]
        print(name, f"scale={scale:.4g}", [float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in d], err)
# e4m3 scale=1 [0.003906, 0.375, 3.0, 20.0, 448.0] [30.2, 1.4, 3.4, 4.8, 25.3]
# e4m3 scale=1.339 [0.002616, 0.3767, 3.013, 21.43, 600.0] [12.8, 1.8, 3.9, 2.0, 0.0]
# e5m2 scale=1 [0.00293, 0.375, 3.0, 20.0, 640.0] [2.3, 1.4, 3.4, 4.8, 6.7]
# e5m2 scale=0.01046 [0.00327, 0.3348, 2.679, 21.43, 600.0] [9.0, 9.5, 7.6, 2.0, 0.0]
blocks.caption: Runs on a CPU (Python 3, NumPy, ml_dtypes); the comments are its real output. The clip mimics the saturating CUDA conversion. The last line shows why calibration is not free for E5M2: a scale chosen only to avoid clipping pushes small values toward its coarse grid.

blocks.md:
**Page bytes.** Lesson 5's formula with $s = 1$: a Llama-3-8B layer page of 16 tokens is $8 \cdot 16 \cdot 256 \cdot 1 = 32{,}768$ bytes, 2,048 bytes per token per layer, and 65,536 bytes (64 KiB) per token over 32 layers, half of the 128 KiB in BF16. A 40 GiB pool then holds 655,360 tokens (40,960 blocks of 16) instead of 327,680.

**Mixed precision changes the block size.** `--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers` keeps some layers in the model's dtype, but the pool still has one page size. vLLM's `_align_heterogeneous_kv_block_size` (in `vllm/platforms/interface.py`) grows the FP8 block until one FP8 page covers a BF16 page at the backend's smallest kernel block: $4{,}096 \cdot 16 = 65{,}536$ bytes, so FP8 layers use 32-token blocks, and logs *Setting attention block size to 32 tokens*. The docs add that such pools zero newly allocated blocks before use.

blocks.title: Llama-3-8B tokens in a 40 GiB KV pool

scenes.caption: 131,072 bytes per token in BF16 against 65,536 in FP8: twice the tokens in the same memory.
Skipping 16 of 32 layers costs 16 x 4,096 + 16 x 2,048 = 98,304 bytes per token: 436,906 tokens. Simplified: block rounding ignored.

blocks.md: An FP8 cache can silently move you to another backend. On an A100 (FA2), FLASH_ATTN fails validation for any FP8 cache and selection falls to FLASHINFER. On an H100, `fp8_e5m2` does the same. If you also pinned `--attention-backend FLASH_ATTN`, startup fails instead. Check the selector's log line after changing the cache dtype.

A backend handles FP8 in three places: it declares which FP8 dtypes it accepts, its cache write divides by the layer's scale and saturates, and its kernel multiplies by a descale (and, with FA3, takes an FP8 query). The scales belong to the layer, not the backend.

blocks.question: Why do calibrated scales matter more for an E4M3 cache than for E5M2?
options: E4M3 has fewer mantissa bits, so it rounds more coarsely
With the default scale of 1.0, E4M3 saturates any value above 448, while E5M2 reaches 57,344 and rarely clips
Only E4M3 supports per-head scales
E5M2 caches are dequantized in the model's dtype, so scales are ignored
blocks.explain: E4M3 has the extra mantissa bit, so it is the more precise format. Its weakness is range: an outlier key or value above 448 times the scale is clipped, as 600 became 448 above. E5M2's range makes scale 1.0 safe from clipping; per-head scales are a FLASH_ATTN feature, not a format property.

blocks.question: H100, Llama-3-8B in BF16, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e5m2`, no backend pinned. Which backend serves it?
options: FLASH_ATTN, with keys converted to E4M3 on the fly
TRITON_ATTN, because only Triton handles E5M2 on Hopper
Startup fails: no CUDA backend supports E5M2
FLASHINFER, the next entry in the priority list, because FLASH_ATTN never accepts E5M2

lessons.title: Hybrid models and KV cache groups: one pool, many block tables

blocks.md:
Take a toy model with 4 full-attention layers and 4 sliding-window layers of window W = 32, block size 16. At token 112, a full layer looks at all 113 keys, but a sliding layer only at the last 32. Keeping the old keys for the sliding layers would waste memory, so they should be freed while the full layers keep theirs.

Real *hybrid* models mix layer types this way. The design doc lists sliding window plus full attention (gpt-oss, Gemma 2 and 3, Ministral, Cohere), Mamba plus full attention (Bamba, Jamba, MiniMax) and chunked local plus full attention (Llama 4). *LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management* (lesson 4) introduced the allocator for them; *PagedAttention and prefix caching* (lesson 5) has the prefix-cache rules; Mamba state itself is outside this course. Here: what the backends see.

A recap in two sentences. The hybrid KV cache manager splits layers into **KV cache groups**: layers of one attention type that share block ids, so they need the same number of blocks per request. Every group has the same page size, num_layers x block_size x kv_hidden_size bytes, so blocks from one pool fit any group.

Our toy has group 0 (4 full layers) and group 1 (4 sliding layers). With a Llama-3-8B layer shape (4,096 bytes per token per layer) one page is 4 x 16 x 4,096 = 262,144 bytes. The consequence for backends: **each group has its own block table and its own slot_mapping**. The runner keeps slot mappings as a [num_groups, num_tokens] tensor, and each layer's cache-write op looks up the row for its layer.

blocks.title: Two block tables for one request (W = 32, block 16)

scenes.caption: A 112-token prompt prefilled in one step. Both groups allocate 7 blocks. Nothing is freed yet: freeing happens before the next allocation, based on the tokens already computed.

First decode step (112 computed). The next token at position 112 sees 81 to 112, so tokens 0 to 80 are skipped and 81 // 16 = 5 whole blocks are freed. Their entries become the null block, id 0. Both groups append an eighth block (ids 15, 16) for position 112.
127 computed: the window for position 127 is 96 to 127, so block 13 (positions 80 to 95) goes too. The sliding group now holds 2 blocks while the full group holds 8.
128 computed: position 128 starts a new block in both tables. Sliding: 3 live blocks, full: 9. Simplified: real block ids come from a free queue, and freeing can lag a step under async scheduling.

blocks.md:
The rule from `SlidingWindowManager`: with c tokens computed, the next token needs positions from c - (W - 1) on, so c - (W - 1) tokens are skipped and the whole blocks among them are freed and replaced by the null block, a placeholder with id 0 that is never handed out. The design doc's own example matches: block 16, window 32, a 112-token request needs 7 blocks for full attention and 2 for each sliding-window group: the 2 are blocks 13 and 14 in the figure once the out-of-window ones are freed.

Over a long request the saving is large. At 4,096 computed tokens the full group holds 257 blocks and the sliding group 3, so the request uses 260 blocks instead of the 514 it would need if both groups were full attention: 49.4% fewer.

**How groups reach the backends.** Within each KV cache group, the runner creates an `AttentionGroup` per backend (and per layer spec and query-head count), and gives it its own metadata builder. Each step, for each group, it fills a `CommonAttentionMetadata` with *that group's* `block_table_tensor` and `slot_mapping` and calls the builder. So lesson 1's "once per step per KV cache group" is, precisely, once per attention group. Layers in a group share the result.

The window reaches the kernel from the layer, not the group: FLASH_ATTN passes the impl's own `(W - 1, 0)`. The source says why: with the hybrid manager disabled, one group can hold windowed and global layers together (Gemma-3 is the example given), and the group cannot describe both.

**A different backend per group.** `AttentionConfig.backend_per_kind` maps a group kind to a backend. The kinds come from `KVCacheSpecKind`: `full_attention`, `mla_attention`, `sliding_window`, `sliding_window_mla`, `mamba`, `chunked_local_attention` and a few more. Kinds you do not list fall back to `backend` or to automatic selection, and an override that is invalid for its kind raises at startup.

Freedom stops at the shared pool: all backends still have to agree on one KV cache layout (lesson 5) and run on the group's block size.

blocks.md: **When the group's block is too big for the kernel.** In a Mamba hybrid, the attention block size is raised until an attention page is as large as a Mamba state page; the design doc warns this can exceed 400 tokens. FlashMLA, for one, runs only 64-token blocks. vLLM handles this with *kernel blocks*: the backend gets a smaller `kernel_block_size` that divides the manager's, and each manager block b becomes kernel blocks b x r + j for j from 0 to r - 1, where r is the size ratio (`map_to_kernel_block_table`). The cache view is reshaped to match, so slot numbers do not change.

blocks.title: Manager blocks of 64 tokens as kernel blocks of 16

scenes.caption: One request's table from the KV cache manager: blocks 3 and 9, 64 tokens each. The backend only supports 16-token blocks, so r = 64 / 16 = 4.
Each manager block expands to 4 consecutive kernel blocks: 3 becomes 12 to 15, 9 becomes 36 to 39. The builder sees this 8-entry table and never learns the manager used 64.
Position 100 is in manager block 9 at offset 36, slot 9 x 64 + 36 = 612. In kernel terms it is kernel block 36 + 36 // 16 = 38, offset 4: slot 38 x 16 + 4 = 612. Same slot.

blocks.md: A sliding-window group's block table is full of null entries. A backend that ignores the window and reads every position up to `seq_lens` will read block 0, which holds nothing meaningful. Supporting `supports_sliding_window` means honoring the window in the kernel, not just accepting the argument.

Hybrid models give each KV cache group its own block table and slot mapping, so the builder runs per attention group and can even be a different backend per group. What stays shared is the pool: one page size, one layout, and kernel blocks when a backend needs smaller ones.

blocks.question: A new request shares a 200-token prefix with an earlier one, but the cached block holding tokens 0 to 15 was evicted. Why can the sliding-window group (W = 32) still reuse the prefix while the full-attention group cannot?
options: The sliding group only needs the last W - 1 tokens before the hit point to be cached; the full group needs every block from token 0
Sliding-window blocks are never evicted
The full-attention group recomputes evicted blocks in place without a prefill
Both groups can reuse it, because the hit is taken from the longer group
blocks.explain: From the design doc: a full-attention hit needs every prefix token cached, scanned left to right, while a sliding-window hit needs only the last window. The request's hit is the intersection over groups, so here it is limited by the full group. The prefix-caching course covers the scan.

blocks.question: Manager block size 128, a backend that runs 32-token kernel blocks, and a manager table [5, 2]. Which kernel block holds position 200?
options: Kernel block 10
Kernel block 6
Kernel block 22
blocks.explain: r = 128 / 32 = 4, so manager block 2 becomes kernel blocks 8 to 11. Position 200 is at table index 200 // 128 = 1 (block id 2), offset 72, and 72 // 32 = 2, so kernel block 2 x 4 + 2 = 10. Using the table index instead of the id gives 6; using block 5 gives 22; 328 is a slot-like number, not a block.

lessons.title: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades

blocks.md: A decode step for a small model is hundreds of short kernels, and launching them from Python can take longer than running them. A **CUDA graph** records a sequence of kernel launches once and replays it with a single launch. It freezes three things: tensor shapes, tensor addresses and any host-side choice made during recording. Attention is where all three bite. The batch size changes every step, metadata must live in persistent buffers, and many backends pick a different kernel for prefill than for decode.

vLLM handles shape with **padding**. Graphs are captured for a list of token counts, and a batch is padded up to the next captured size. By default the largest size is $\min(2 \cdot S \cdot q_{dec}, 512)$, or 1,024 on data-center Blackwell, and never more than `max_num_batched_tokens` (which is itself captured when it fits), where $S$ is `max_num_seqs`, the most requests one step may hold and $q_{dec}$ is the uniform decode query length (1 without speculative decoding). Speculative decoding has a cheap draft propose $k$ tokens and the model check all of them in one step, so each request runs $1 + k$ query tokens. The sizes are 1, 2, 4, then multiples of 8 below 256, then multiples of 16 up to the maximum.

With `max_num_seqs = 256` and no speculation, that is 51 sizes from 1 to 512: the 3 small sizes, 31 multiples of 8 from 8 to 248, and 17 multiples of 16 from 256 to 512. Padded rows get `PAD_SLOT_ID = -1` in `slot_mapping`, and padded requests get query length 0. A batch larger than the maximum runs eagerly, meaning its kernels are launched one by one from Python with no graph.

blocks.md:
Kernel choice is handled by **declared support**. Each builder reports an `AttentionCGSupport`:

- `ALWAYS`: any batch, mixed prefill and decode included, can replay a full graph.
- `UNIFORM_BATCH`: only batches where every request has the same query length, such as plain decode or speculative verification with $1 + k$ tokens.
- `UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE`: only batches where every query length is 1.
- `NEVER`: no full graphs.

The model's level is the minimum over all its backends.

blocks.title: Which batches can replay a full CUDA graph (source on main)

scenes.caption: 1 means a full graph is allowed. FA3, FA4, Triton and FlashInfer-MLA report ALWAYS. FA2 reports UNIFORM_BATCH on purpose: the source says this pushes vLLM to FULL_AND_PIECEWISE for performance.
FlashInfer reports UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE unless its TRTLLM decode path is usable for the head geometry, which raises it to UNIFORM_BATCH. CUTLASS_MLA captures single-token decode only.
Speculative decoding verifies 1 + k tokens per request, the middle column. Rows with 0 there cannot capture those batches as full graphs.

blocks.md:
vLLM's `-O` flag sets an optimization level from 0 to 3. At `-O2`, the default, the graph mode is `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`. A uniform decode batch replays a full graph that includes attention. Any other batch replays **piecewise** graphs: the model is split at attention, the non-attention pieces are graphs, and attention runs eagerly between them, so it can use any kernel. `CudaGraphManager.dispatch` (in the runner's `cudagraph_utils.py`) tries a uniform-decode FULL graph first, then the smallest compatible graph keyed by token count, and otherwise runs eagerly (NONE).

The split is made by torch.compile. Attention is wrapped in the custom op `vllm::unified_attention_with_output`, which the compiler treats as opaque, and by default that op (plus the cache-write op `vllm::unified_kv_cache_update`) is listed in `splitting_ops`. The captured graph is cut at every such op. For a 32-layer model that leaves a piece before layer 0's attention, a piece between each pair of attention calls (output projection, MLP, next layer's QKV), and a piece after the last one.

blocks.md:
When the requested mode asks for more than the backends allow, `resolve_cudagraph_mode_and_sizes` downgrades it and logs a warning:

- Full graphs for mixed batches without `ALWAYS` become `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, or `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` if attention is not a split point. With `NEVER`, this request raises an error instead.
- Full decode graphs with `NEVER` become `PIECEWISE`, or `NONE`.
- Speculative decoding ($q_{dec} > 1$) with support below `UNIFORM_BATCH` becomes `PIECEWISE`, or `NONE`, because the decode graph would be wrong for $1 + k$ token queries.

Graph capture assumes `forward` does the same thing at replay as at capture. That is why `AttentionImpl.forward` must not branch on Python values that change per batch inside a full graph, and why builders write into persistent buffers instead of allocating new tensors.

CUDA graphs constrain attention through shape (pad to a captured size), address (persistent metadata buffers) and kernel choice (`AttentionCGSupport`). The weakest backend in the model sets the graph mode for everyone.

blocks.question: A model runs FLASHINFER without the TRTLLM path, so it reports UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE. You turn on speculative decoding with 3 draft tokens. What does vLLM do with the default FULL_AND_PIECEWISE mode?
options: Captures full graphs for 4-token verification batches anyway
Downgrades to PIECEWISE (attention is a split point), so verification batches run attention eagerly
Raises an error at startup
Switches the backend to FLASH_ATTN automatically
blocks.explain: With a uniform decode length of 4 and support below UNIFORM_BATCH, the resolver logs that the mode is not supported with spec decode and sets PIECEWISE when attention is in the splitting ops. It never swaps backends: selection is already finished by then.

blocks.question: With `max_num_seqs = 256` (max capture size 512), which batch wastes the largest *fraction* of its padded graph?
options: 257 tokens
100 tokens
9 tokens
511 tokens
blocks.explain: 9 pads to 16, wasting 7 of 16 rows (43.8%). 257 pads to 272 (5.5%), 100 to 104 (3.8%) and 511 to 512 (0.2%). Small batches matter most for latency, which is why `performance_mode = interactivity` captures every size from 1 to 32.
